public_rationale: NIST supports the concern that hallucinations complicate consequential use. Mathematical research establishes limits under particular assumptions, but those limits do not establish that new branches of mathematics are necessary. Other research explicitly cautions against universal inevitability and discusses abstention. None of the reviewed evidence demonstrates general elimination under the contract. The practical concern has support; the stronger necessity claim remains unsettled.
limitations: Impossibility theorems depend on their model classes and assumptions.
Avoiding answers or restricting a task can change what elimination means.
The available source-type vocabulary classifies the NIST guidance as official_statistics, although it is risk guidance rather than a statistical release.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Hallucinations cannot be resolved without new branches of mathematics, and they make it hard for business-critical applications to rely on generative AI.

statement.excerpt: Hallucinations — which occur when models authoritatively states something that isn't true (or in the case of an image or a video makes something that looks...wrong) — are impossible to resolve without new branches of mathematics, and while you might be able to reduce or mitigate them, their existence makes it hard for business-critical applications to truly rely on generative AI.

from_speaker: impossible to resolve without new branches of mathematics
hard for business-critical applications to truly rely on generative AI
our_interpretation: Because the speaker explicitly distinguishes mitigation, read 'resolve' as eliminating hallucinations in useful general-purpose operation, not merely reducing their frequency.
Read 'new branches of mathematics' as mathematical foundations unavailable when the post was published, rather than any new algorithm using established mathematics.
The claim combines a necessary-condition assertion about elimination with a practical assertion about consequential deployment.

This is a causal and mathematical assertion, not a conditional forecast with a deadline. Later research may address the asserted necessity, but later model performance cannot by itself establish the reliability of September 2024 systems.
criteria.support_condition: A sound result establishes that the relevant elimination goal cannot be achieved using existing mathematical foundations, and deployment evidence shows hallucinations materially obstruct reliable consequential use.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A reproducible, appropriately general elimination method using existing mathematics refutes the necessity claim. Reliable bounded applications alone do not refute the claim that hallucinations make reliance difficult.

evidence.excerpt:
Risks of confabulated content may be especially important to monitor when integrating GAI
into applications involving consequential decision making.
evidence.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
evidence.explanation: Supports the practical concern about relying on generative AI for consequential decisions. This is official risk guidance, not proof that new mathematics is necessary.

evidence.excerpt: In this paper, we formalize the problem and show that it is impossible to eliminate hallucination in LLMs.
evidence.publisher: arXiv; Ziwei Xu, Sanjay Jain and Mohan Kankanhalli
evidence.explanation: The argument concerns learning computable ground-truth functions in a specified formal world. It supports limits on universal correctness but does not identify a necessary new branch of mathematics or establish the same result for every practical deployment.

evidence.excerpt: It should not be taken to mean that hallucination is inevitable.
evidence.publisher: Adam Tauman Kalai and Santosh S. Vempala; STOC 2024 manuscript on arXiv
evidence.explanation: The authors explicitly caution against treating their statistical lower bound for calibrated predictors as universal inevitability. This limits an argument for necessity but does not demonstrate general elimination.

evidence.excerpt: They are not, because language models can abstain when uncertain.
evidence.explanation: The research summary presents abstention as a reason hallucinations are not inevitable. It also acknowledges remaining hallucinations, so it is not evidence that a useful general-purpose system has eliminated them.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A precise elimination goal and either a sound necessity theorem covering that goal or a reproducible counterexample using established mathematics.
